# black_hole — a learning fork by Lorkyrr

Hi, I'm **Lorkyrr**. This repository is my personal fork of
[kavan010/black_hole](https://github.com/kavan010/black_hole), a real-time black hole simulation
(gravitational lensing, accretion disk and a curved spacetime grid, ray-traced on the GPU).

I did **not** write the simulation. All credit for the original idea, the physics and the first implementation goes to
**kavan010**. This fork is where I use that project as a playground to learn new tools.

## Read this first: AI was used, on purpose

**Most of the code added in this fork was generated by an AI assistant (Claude Code), working under my direction.**
That includes the Vulkan renderer, the Go port, the Rust port, the Python port, the Dockerfile, the CMake changes and the documentation.

I am saying this plainly because it matters for how you read this repository:

- It is **not** a showcase of code I wrote by hand, and it should not be judged as one.
- It is **a base for learning**. I used the AI to get a working starting point for things I did not know yet, and I am
  learning **Vulkan, Go and Rust "the hard way"** from there: reading every line, breaking things on purpose, fixing them,
  and rewriting parts myself.
- The documents next to the code were written for exactly that: they explain *what* was done, *why*, and give a step-by-step
  tutorial to redo each port from scratch (see [Documentation](#documentation)).
- Things are only claimed as verified when they were actually run. What was **not** verified is listed in each port's document.

## What I wanted

I wanted a real project to learn three things at once, without inventing a toy example:

1. **Vulkan**: a low-level graphics API where nothing is implicit (memory, synchronization, image layouts).
2. **Go**: a language I wanted to try on something graphical, with cgo and OpenGL.
3. **Rust**: the same, but with a modern GPU abstraction (wgpu) and the borrow checker.

A black hole ray tracer is a good fit: the core is one compute shader, the CPU side is small and well defined, and the result is
easy to compare across implementations. Porting the **same** simulation three times makes the differences between the
approaches visible, instead of the differences between the programs.

## What this fork is for

It is a study fork, not a replacement for the upstream project. It contains the same 3D simulation implemented four ways:

| Folder | Language | Graphics API | What it teaches |
|---|---|---|---|
| [`C++/`](C++/) | C++17 | **Vulkan 1.3** (dynamic rendering, synchronization2) | explicit GPU programming: swapchain, descriptors, pipelines, barriers |
| [`Go/`](Go/) | Go | OpenGL 4.3 (via cgo, `go-gl`) | Go modules, packages, `embed`, cgo, testing the CPU side without a GPU |
| [`Rust/`](Rust/) | Rust (edition 2024) | **wgpu** (Vulkan underneath), WGSL shaders | safe GPU code, `bytemuck`, `winit` 0.30, what wgpu automates compared to raw Vulkan |
| [`Python/`](Python/) | Python 3.12+ (managed by `uv`) | **Vulkan 1.3** (raw, via the `vulkan` cffi bindings), GLFW on Wayland | the same Vulkan renderer as `C++/` line by line, in a high-level language; `uv`, cffi, testing std140 layouts without a GPU |

All four share the same design: a **graphics-free simulation layer** (camera, Newtonian gravity, grid mesh) separated from the
renderer, and the same pipeline: compute shader (geodesics) → 200×150 texture → full-screen quad, drawn over a warped spacetime grid.

## What changed compared to upstream

- Added the Vulkan 1.3 renderer, the Go, Rust and Python ports, each with its own tests or build.
- Moved the C++ code into `C++/` and added a `Dockerfile` for the Vulkan build.
- **Made the fork Linux-only and Vulkan-only on the C++ side.** I removed the Windows leftovers (`black_hole.exe`, `vs_code/`,
  `vcpkg.json`) and the original OpenGL C++ programs (`2D_lensing.cpp`, `CPU-geodesic.cpp`, `ray_tracing.cpp`, `black_hole.cpp`
  and their GL shaders). They still exist upstream and in this repository's git history. I removed them because this fork is about
  learning Vulkan, and carrying a parallel OpenGL version I do not use only added noise.
- Added documentation: what was done, why, and a tutorial for each port.

Not touched: `Gravity_Sim.zip` (old code from the original author).

## Quick start

All commands assume Debian/Ubuntu and a GPU with working Vulkan drivers (`vulkaninfo --summary` should list your GPU).

### C++ / Vulkan

```bash
sudo apt install build-essential cmake libglfw3-dev libglm-dev libvulkan-dev glslc \
                 vulkan-validationlayers mesa-vulkan-drivers
cd C++
cmake -B build -S . && cmake --build build
cd build && ./black_hole_cpp          # must run from here: it loads the .spv shaders from the working directory
```

Without `-DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release` the Vulkan validation layer is enabled if installed. Docker alternative:
see the header of [`C++/Dockerfile`](C++/Dockerfile).

### Go / OpenGL 4.3

```bash
sudo apt install build-essential libgl1-mesa-dev libegl-dev libwayland-dev libxkbcommon-dev
cd Go
go run -tags wayland .                # native Wayland. On X11 install xorg-dev and drop the tag
go test ./sim/                        # CPU-side physics and camera, no GPU needed
```

### Rust / wgpu

```bash
cd Rust
cargo run --release
cargo test
```

### Python / Vulkan

```bash
sudo apt install glslc vulkan-validationlayers mesa-vulkan-drivers   # Ubuntu 26.04+, Wayland session
cd Python
uv run main.py                        # uv installs Python deps (vulkan, glfw, numpy) on first run
uv run pytest                         # CPU-side physics, camera and UBO layouts, no GPU needed
```

### Controls (same in all four)

| Input | Action |
|---|---|
| Left mouse button + drag (Go, Rust and Python: middle button too) | orbit the camera |
| Mouse wheel | zoom |
| `G` | toggle gravity between the objects |
| Right mouse button | gravity while held |
| `Esc` (Go, Rust) or close the window | quit |

## Honest status

- **Verified:** the Vulkan build runs on an NVIDIA RTX 3050 with zero validation-layer messages, and was compared pixel by pixel against
  the original OpenGL output (0.7% of pixels differ, explained in `C++/PORT_VULKAN.md`). Go `sim` tests and the Rust tests pass.
  The Go program builds and passes `go vet`; the Rust program ran for a few seconds without crashing (neither was run interactively).
- **Python port:** ran 60 frames on the RTX 3050 under Wayland with zero validation-layer messages, and a captured frame looked right;
  not compared pixel by pixel against C++ (details in `Python/PORT_PYTHON.md`).
- **Not verified:** the Go, Rust and Python images were not compared against the C++ output; window resizing; macOS; Intel/AMD hardware
  (beyond a software/RADV run of the Vulkan version); long interactive sessions.
- Vulkan does **not** make the simulation faster than OpenGL here. The bottleneck is the compute shader (60,000 steps per pixel),
  which is the same work in every API. The value of the port is control and learning.
